# URI students receive Black Scholar Awards for outstanding achievement

[![Image 2: Christopher Hunter](https://www.uri.edu/news/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/hunter.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/hunter.jpg)

Christopher Hunter, associate professor of civil engineering, speaking to the audience at the Black Scholar Awards. Photo by Michael Salerno. 

KINGSTON, R.I., May 3, 2018—Sixteen University of Rhode Island students were honored for their academic and community achievements at the University’s 21st annual Black Scholar Awards.

Established by Donald Cunnigen, URI professor of sociology and anthropology, the awards recognize African-American students for their outstanding achievements at URI and beyond.

The students received the awards April 24 during a ceremony on the Kingston campus that was coordinated by Christopher Hunter, associate professor of civil engineering.

Here’s a list of the recipients:

**William Gould Award for All-Around Outstanding Achievement**

[![Image 3: Kendall Moore and Chelsea Opong-Wadeer](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/MooreOpong-Wadeer-0002-3.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/MooreOpong-Wadeer-0002-3.jpg)

Kendall Moore, journalism professor, and Chelsea Opong-Wadeer. Photo by Michael Salerno

Chelsea Opong-Wadeer, of **Flanders**, **N.J.,** is the daughter of parents who moved to the United States from Ghana in the 1980s. Opong-Wadeer is majoring in journalism with minors in leadership studies and gender and women’s studies. A member of the Dean’s List since her freshman year, Opong-Wadeer is also in the URI Honors Program. She is a URI 101 mentor; a host for a multicultural program for accepted students; and a member of the Student Entertainment Committee. She’s been a reporter for the Good 5 Cent Cigar, her hometown paper and national websites. She interned at Channel 10 in Providence. After graduation, she hopes to get a job at MTV in New York as a production assistant or news writer.

**Arthur L. Hardge Award for All-Around Outstanding Community Service**

Africa Smith, of **Providence**, is majoring in political science and Africana studies with a

[![Image 4: Marc Hardge and Africa Smith](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/HardgeSmith0003-1.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/HardgeSmith0003-1.jpg)

Marc Hardge, academic adviser, University College, and Africa Smith. Photo by Michael Salerno

minor in law, politics and society. She is in the Honor’s and Talent Development programs. She’s been a resident advisor, a URI 101 mentor and a URI orientation leader. One major experience that she valued was her mayoral fellowship in Providence. She also received certification at URI in Nonviolence Conflict Reconciliation.

[![Image 5: Mario McClain](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/Mario-McClain1.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/Mario-McClain1.jpg)

Mario McClain. Photo by Michael Salerno

Mario McClain, of **Cranston**, has been a leader and mentor at URI. He has worked as a residential assistant and an orientation leader for freshmen. He was a founding member and president of the Police Student Advisory Committee, where he worked to strengthen the relationship between students of color and the police. As a member of Brothers On A New Direction, or BOND, he mentored adolescent students of color from inner-city middle schools and high schools and volunteered in the community.

**Martin Luther King, Jr. Award for Outstanding Leadership and Contribution to the University Community**

Selena Evora, of **Pawtucket**, is double majoring in health studies and gender and women’s studies, and minoring in leadership studies. She is the first African-American president of the Phi Sigma Sigma Sorority at URI. As a part of the Cape Verdean Student Association, she was a community service chair. She was a student coordinator for the Peer’s Learning Educating and Supporting Everyone Program for the URI Women’s Center. She was a URI 101 mentor and resident adviser. She worked as a teaching assistant for the Rose Butler Browne Mentoring Course, and she is president of the Multicultural Unity and Student Involvement Council.

[![Image 6: Photo by Michael Salerno](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/QuainooAntoine0004.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/QuainooAntoine0004.jpg)

Vanessa Quainoo, professor communication studies, and Shawn Antoine.

Shawn Antoine, of **New York City**, is a double major in political science and film studies. He’s been a scholar and an activist at URI, as well as a member of the football team. In 2016, he won the Africana Studies Innovation Award and was celebrated as one of the most promising young students in Africana Studies for his first film,[_The Movement: Black Lives Matter_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N4vc-iiiN48&feature=youtu.be)_._ He was a member of the Diversifying Individuals Via Education Conference team and the URI Student Senate and was vice president of the Student Athletic Advisory Committee. In 2016, Antoine received the URI Diversity Award for Arts and Culture. In 2017, he received the Public Relations Excellence Award. His films were selected for seven film festivals with the Amazon Underground Film Festival.

**Harvey Robert Turner Award for Outstanding Service to the University of Rhode Island Black Community**

[![Image 7: Carl-Ernst Rousseau and Tunde Akinkuowo](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/RousseauAkinkuowo0005.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/RousseauAkinkuowo0005.jpg)

Carl-Ernst Rousseau, engineering professor, and Tunde Akinkuowo. Photo by Michael Salerno

Tunde Akinkuowo, of **Providence**, is majoring in industrial and systems engineering. Beyond his classwork, he has taken time to give back to his community by mentoring high school and middle school students of color. He is a member of the National Society of Black Engineers, and he is chair for the Technical Outreach Community Help. He is also involved with the Diversifying Individuals Via Education Conference, a student-led multicultural conference. He has worked on URI’s IT Service Desk, and he interned with Pratt & Whitney, a top engineering company in the aerospace industry. He also conducted research in the microfluidics lab at URI and at North-West University in South Africa, where he worked on a solar car challenge project.

**Jackie Robinson Scholar-Athlete Award**

[![Image 8: Gordon Dash and Mahlik Handley](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/DashHandley0008.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/DashHandley0008.jpg)

Gordon Dash, finance professor, and Mahlik Handley. Photo by Michael Salerno

Mahlik Handley, of **Wakefield,** is a kinesiology major and a champion hammer thrower on the URI track team. He has earned numerous honors and awards at URI, including as an Outdoor A-10 Champion 2014-2016; a member of four A-10 championship teams and two New England championship teams; and a qualifier for the first round of the NCAAs in 2014. He is the 5 th best hammer thrower in URI history. Beyond this, he has served as a student-athlete orientation captain and as a Rhody life skills team captain. This year, he was a team captain, providing leadership, sportsmanship and mentorship support. He completed his degree work in December and is now pursuing a master’s degree in the URI College of Education.

**Sojourner Truth Award for Scholarly Persistence and Dedication**

Jordan Powell, of **Kingwood, Texas**, is majoring in environmental science and

[![Image 9: Gitahi Gititi and Jordan Powell](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/GititiPowell0006.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/GititiPowell0006.jpg)

Gitahi Gititi, professor of English and Africana studies, and Jordan Powell. Photo by Michael Salerno

management, and he is a four-year starter on the URI baseball team. He has received many athletic accomplishments including New England Intercollegiate Baseball Association All New England First Team twice. He was a key contributor to the baseball team’s first-ever NCAA win in 2016, with a multiple hit game. Beyond that, Powell has been a participant in a science and engineering fellowship, and he has volunteered as a student-athlete mentor. He also volunteered for the Nature Conservancy.

Powell experienced a period of adversity when he was hospitalized with a blood infection that became a three-week battle for survival. Even though he was in the hospital, he stayed on top of his work. He never gave in or asked for a medical leave of absence. He took exams and completed papers and earned a spot on the Dean’s List that semester. He went on to compete in the upcoming baseball season.

[![Image 10: Shemaiah Thompson and Yvette Harps-Logan](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/ThompsonHarps-Logan0007.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/ThompsonHarps-Logan0007.jpg)

Shemaiah Thompson and Yvette Harps-Logan, associate professor of textiles, fashion merchandising and design. Photo by Michael Salerno

Shemaiah Thompson, of **Cranston**, is a kinesiology major who has been on the Dean’s List since her freshman year. She was a member of the URI ALIMA dance organization, Seeds of Success, and the Sankofa Campus Ministry. For the past three years, she’s been on the leadership staff of Sankofa, serving as secretary and treasurer. She also has research experience as part of longitudinal study of communication, nutrition and exercise, while testing physical functioning, measuring body composition, administering physical activity questionnaires and dealing with data reduction and entry.

Thompson faced challenges her freshman year when her father was diagnosed with Stage 4 cancer. She traveled home often to help her family and contemplated taking time away from college, but she said the Talent Development community and Sankofa encouraged her to push through.

**Noreen Coachman M.D. Award for Older Student**

[![Image 11: James Haile and Tracie Montgomery](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/HaileMontgomery0012.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/HaileMontgomery0012.jpg)

James Haile, assistant professor philosophy, and Tracie Montgomery. Photo by Michael Salerno

Tracie Montgomery, of **Providence**, is a double major in psychology and Africana studies. She has served the community at multiple levels;worked closely with black faculty and staff and the local African American community; served on the student government board; and traveled to Cabo Verde, where she researched her family’s African genealogy. She will travel again to Cabo Verde to help establish a partnership between Cabo Verde universities and organizations, and URI. She became a member of the Alpha Sigma Lambda Honor Society in May 2017.

**Saint Clair Drake Award for Outstanding Scholarly Research**

Yulyana Torres, of **Providence**, is double majoring

[![Image 12](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/TorresNevius0011.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/TorresNevius0011.jpg)

Yulyana Torres and Marcus Nevius, assistant professor of history. Photos by Michael Salerno

in communications and gender and women’s studies. Her work was acknowledged recently in a scholarly book review essay, “The Dark Past of Rhode Island in New Light.” Torres has undertaken an initiative to bring diversity to the Rhode Island Statehouse. Having interned there and observed the lack of art that reflects the full diversity of the state’s history, Torres has lobbied state officials to purchase a portrait of Rhode Island’s first black regiment, a corps of black soldiers that served with valor during the American Revolution.

**Saint Elmo Brady for Outstanding Achievement in Science**

ThankGod Ugochukw

[![Image 13: Charles Watson and ThankGod Ugochukwu.](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/WatsonUgochukwu0010-1.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/WatsonUgochukwu0010-1.jpg)

Charles Watson, assistant director of diversity in the College of Engineering, and ThankGod Ugochukwu. Photo by Michael Salerno

ThankGod Ugochukw, of **Norwood, Mass**., is a biomedical engineering major. He’s been involved in the Louis Stokes Alliance for Minorities Participation Program, and that has afforded him various opportunities, including conducting research in the biomeasurement and biomedical instrumentation design labs. He interned with 21 st Century Fox, where he helped the engineering team repair damaged technology and worked on interactive programs. He’s been an integral part of the National Society of Black Engineers, serving as president this year.

**David Edmonds Award**

Sierra Jade Clayton, of **Providence**, is a writing and rhetoric major. She is an

[![Image 14: Bob Dilworth and Sierra Jade Clayton](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/DilworthClayton0009.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/DilworthClayton0009.jpg)

Bob Dilworth, art professor, and Sierra Jade Clayton. Photo by Michael Salerno

effective communicator who has demonstrated the ability to establish and maintain sensitive and equitable interpersonal relations, evidenced by her varied experiences working with culturally diverse groups. She is a member of the Rhode Island Chapter of the Lead Program and the National Coalition of 100 Black Women and New Urban Arts, and she is a volunteer for the Diversifying Individuals Via Education Conference. At New Urban Arts, she worked in the development of poetry, fashion, sketching, screen-printing and photography. She also has served as a senior consultant at the Writing and Rhetoric Lab at URI.

**Estes Benson Awards**

[![Image 15: Bryan Dewsbury and Florette Fils Aima, sister of Carine M. Saint Felix.](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/DewsburyFils-Aima0013.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/DewsburyFils-Aima0013.jpg)

Bryan Dewsbury, assistant professor biological sciences, and Florette Fils Aima, sister of Carine M. Saint Felix. Photo by Michael Salerno

Carine M. Saint Felix, a native of **Leogane, Haiti** who lives in **Woonsocket**, is a nursing major. She decided to become a nurse after losing her younger brother, who died suddenly after complaining of cold-like symptoms and was unable to get adequate health care in Haiti. Among her honors and involvement include the Sigma Theta Tau International Honor Society of Nursing; American Psychiatric Nurses Association; American Nurses Association; and Mentor/Educator-Women’s Refugee Center of Rhode Island. After completing her degree, she plans to pursue her master of science degree in nursing.

[![Image 16: Bryan Dewsbury and Pa Sosseh](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/DewsburySosseh0014.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/DewsburySosseh0014.jpg)

Bryan Dewsbury, assistant professor biological sciences, and Pa Sosseh. Photos by Michael Salerno

Pa Sosseh, a native of **Gambia**who lives in**Pawtucket**, came to the United States in 2010 and not long after that, enrolled at the Community College of Rhode Island. Seeking a way to pay tuition, Sosseh joined the Rhode Island National Guard. After completing his basic combat training, Sosseh transferred to URI, where he’s made the Dean’s List every semester. He initially majored in biochemistry, but after a research project through a science and engineering fellowship, he found his passion for molecular biology. He changed his major to medical laboratory science, with the goal of becoming a doctor.

[![Image 17: Alycia Mosley Austin and Danielle Perry](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/AustinPerry0015.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/AustinPerry0015.jpg)

Alycia Mosley Austin, assistant dean for recruitment and diversity initiatives at the Graduate School, and Danielle Perry. Photo by Michael Salerno

**Donald Cunnigen Award**

Danielle Perry, of **Hazlet, N.J**., is a third-year Ph.D. student in the biological and environmental sciences program. Her work focuses on the environmental stressors impacting coastal ecosystems. In addition to her research interests in marine conservation, Perry interns at the Save the Bay Center in Westerly. She mentors undergraduates through the RI-EPSCoR Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship program and as a teaching assistant in the College of the Environmental and Life Sciences. She strives to expose young people of color to opportunities in science, technology, engineering and math careers.

# URI students receive Black Scholar Awards for outstanding achievement

[![Image 2: Christopher Hunter](https://www.uri.edu/news/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/hunter.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/hunter.jpg)

Christopher Hunter, associate professor of civil engineering, speaking to the audience at the Black Scholar Awards. Photo by Michael Salerno. 

KINGSTON, R.I., May 3, 2018—Sixteen University of Rhode Island students were honored for their academic and community achievements at the University’s 21st annual Black Scholar Awards.

Established by Donald Cunnigen, URI professor of sociology and anthropology, the awards recognize African-American students for their outstanding achievements at URI and beyond.

The students received the awards April 24 during a ceremony on the Kingston campus that was coordinated by Christopher Hunter, associate professor of civil engineering.

Here’s a list of the recipients:

**William Gould Award for All-Around Outstanding Achievement**

[![Image 3: Kendall Moore and Chelsea Opong-Wadeer](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/MooreOpong-Wadeer-0002-3.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/MooreOpong-Wadeer-0002-3.jpg)

Kendall Moore, journalism professor, and Chelsea Opong-Wadeer. Photo by Michael Salerno

Chelsea Opong-Wadeer, of **Flanders**, **N.J.,** is the daughter of parents who moved to the United States from Ghana in the 1980s. Opong-Wadeer is majoring in journalism with minors in leadership studies and gender and women’s studies. A member of the Dean’s List since her freshman year, Opong-Wadeer is also in the URI Honors Program. She is a URI 101 mentor; a host for a multicultural program for accepted students; and a member of the Student Entertainment Committee. She’s been a reporter for the Good 5 Cent Cigar, her hometown paper and national websites. She interned at Channel 10 in Providence. After graduation, she hopes to get a job at MTV in New York as a production assistant or news writer.

**Arthur L. Hardge Award for All-Around Outstanding Community Service**

Africa Smith, of **Providence**, is majoring in political science and Africana studies with a

[![Image 4: Marc Hardge and Africa Smith](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/HardgeSmith0003-1.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/HardgeSmith0003-1.jpg)

Marc Hardge, academic adviser, University College, and Africa Smith. Photo by Michael Salerno

minor in law, politics and society. She is in the Honor’s and Talent Development programs. She’s been a resident advisor, a URI 101 mentor and a URI orientation leader. One major experience that she valued was her mayoral fellowship in Providence. She also received certification at URI in Nonviolence Conflict Reconciliation.

[![Image 5: Mario McClain](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/Mario-McClain1.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/Mario-McClain1.jpg)

Mario McClain. Photo by Michael Salerno

Mario McClain, of **Cranston**, has been a leader and mentor at URI. He has worked as a residential assistant and an orientation leader for freshmen. He was a founding member and president of the Police Student Advisory Committee, where he worked to strengthen the relationship between students of color and the police. As a member of Brothers On A New Direction, or BOND, he mentored adolescent students of color from inner-city middle schools and high schools and volunteered in the community.

**Martin Luther King, Jr. Award for Outstanding Leadership and Contribution to the University Community**

Selena Evora, of **Pawtucket**, is double majoring in health studies and gender and women’s studies, and minoring in leadership studies. She is the first African-American president of the Phi Sigma Sigma Sorority at URI. As a part of the Cape Verdean Student Association, she was a community service chair. She was a student coordinator for the Peer’s Learning Educating and Supporting Everyone Program for the URI Women’s Center. She was a URI 101 mentor and resident adviser. She worked as a teaching assistant for the Rose Butler Browne Mentoring Course, and she is president of the Multicultural Unity and Student Involvement Council.

[![Image 6: Photo by Michael Salerno](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/QuainooAntoine0004.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/QuainooAntoine0004.jpg)

Vanessa Quainoo, professor communication studies, and Shawn Antoine.

Shawn Antoine, of **New York City**, is a double major in political science and film studies. He’s been a scholar and an activist at URI, as well as a member of the football team. In 2016, he won the Africana Studies Innovation Award and was celebrated as one of the most promising young students in Africana Studies for his first film,[_The Movement: Black Lives Matter_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N4vc-iiiN48&feature=youtu.be)_._ He was a member of the Diversifying Individuals Via Education Conference team and the URI Student Senate and was vice president of the Student Athletic Advisory Committee. In 2016, Antoine received the URI Diversity Award for Arts and Culture. In 2017, he received the Public Relations Excellence Award. His films were selected for seven film festivals with the Amazon Underground Film Festival.

**Harvey Robert Turner Award for Outstanding Service to the University of Rhode Island Black Community**

[![Image 7: Carl-Ernst Rousseau and Tunde Akinkuowo](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/RousseauAkinkuowo0005.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/RousseauAkinkuowo0005.jpg)

Carl-Ernst Rousseau, engineering professor, and Tunde Akinkuowo. Photo by Michael Salerno

Tunde Akinkuowo, of **Providence**, is majoring in industrial and systems engineering. Beyond his classwork, he has taken time to give back to his community by mentoring high school and middle school students of color. He is a member of the National Society of Black Engineers, and he is chair for the Technical Outreach Community Help. He is also involved with the Diversifying Individuals Via Education Conference, a student-led multicultural conference. He has worked on URI’s IT Service Desk, and he interned with Pratt & Whitney, a top engineering company in the aerospace industry. He also conducted research in the microfluidics lab at URI and at North-West University in South Africa, where he worked on a solar car challenge project.

**Jackie Robinson Scholar-Athlete Award**

[![Image 8: Gordon Dash and Mahlik Handley](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/DashHandley0008.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/DashHandley0008.jpg)

Gordon Dash, finance professor, and Mahlik Handley. Photo by Michael Salerno

Mahlik Handley, of **Wakefield,** is a kinesiology major and a champion hammer thrower on the URI track team. He has earned numerous honors and awards at URI, including as an Outdoor A-10 Champion 2014-2016; a member of four A-10 championship teams and two New England championship teams; and a qualifier for the first round of the NCAAs in 2014. He is the 5 th best hammer thrower in URI history. Beyond this, he has served as a student-athlete orientation captain and as a Rhody life skills team captain. This year, he was a team captain, providing leadership, sportsmanship and mentorship support. He completed his degree work in December and is now pursuing a master’s degree in the URI College of Education.

**Sojourner Truth Award for Scholarly Persistence and Dedication**

Jordan Powell, of **Kingwood, Texas**, is majoring in environmental science and

[![Image 9: Gitahi Gititi and Jordan Powell](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/GititiPowell0006.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/GititiPowell0006.jpg)

Gitahi Gititi, professor of English and Africana studies, and Jordan Powell. Photo by Michael Salerno

management, and he is a four-year starter on the URI baseball team. He has received many athletic accomplishments including New England Intercollegiate Baseball Association All New England First Team twice. He was a key contributor to the baseball team’s first-ever NCAA win in 2016, with a multiple hit game. Beyond that, Powell has been a participant in a science and engineering fellowship, and he has volunteered as a student-athlete mentor. He also volunteered for the Nature Conservancy.

Powell experienced a period of adversity when he was hospitalized with a blood infection that became a three-week battle for survival. Even though he was in the hospital, he stayed on top of his work. He never gave in or asked for a medical leave of absence. He took exams and completed papers and earned a spot on the Dean’s List that semester. He went on to compete in the upcoming baseball season.

[![Image 10: Shemaiah Thompson and Yvette Harps-Logan](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/ThompsonHarps-Logan0007.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/ThompsonHarps-Logan0007.jpg)

Shemaiah Thompson and Yvette Harps-Logan, associate professor of textiles, fashion merchandising and design. Photo by Michael Salerno

Shemaiah Thompson, of **Cranston**, is a kinesiology major who has been on the Dean’s List since her freshman year. She was a member of the URI ALIMA dance organization, Seeds of Success, and the Sankofa Campus Ministry. For the past three years, she’s been on the leadership staff of Sankofa, serving as secretary and treasurer. She also has research experience as part of longitudinal study of communication, nutrition and exercise, while testing physical functioning, measuring body composition, administering physical activity questionnaires and dealing with data reduction and entry.

Thompson faced challenges her freshman year when her father was diagnosed with Stage 4 cancer. She traveled home often to help her family and contemplated taking time away from college, but she said the Talent Development community and Sankofa encouraged her to push through.

**Noreen Coachman M.D. Award for Older Student**

[![Image 11: James Haile and Tracie Montgomery](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/HaileMontgomery0012.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/HaileMontgomery0012.jpg)

James Haile, assistant professor philosophy, and Tracie Montgomery. Photo by Michael Salerno

Tracie Montgomery, of **Providence**, is a double major in psychology and Africana studies. She has served the community at multiple levels;worked closely with black faculty and staff and the local African American community; served on the student government board; and traveled to Cabo Verde, where she researched her family’s African genealogy. She will travel again to Cabo Verde to help establish a partnership between Cabo Verde universities and organizations, and URI. She became a member of the Alpha Sigma Lambda Honor Society in May 2017.

**Saint Clair Drake Award for Outstanding Scholarly Research**

Yulyana Torres, of **Providence**, is double majoring

[![Image 12](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/TorresNevius0011.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/TorresNevius0011.jpg)

Yulyana Torres and Marcus Nevius, assistant professor of history. Photos by Michael Salerno

in communications and gender and women’s studies. Her work was acknowledged recently in a scholarly book review essay, “The Dark Past of Rhode Island in New Light.” Torres has undertaken an initiative to bring diversity to the Rhode Island Statehouse. Having interned there and observed the lack of art that reflects the full diversity of the state’s history, Torres has lobbied state officials to purchase a portrait of Rhode Island’s first black regiment, a corps of black soldiers that served with valor during the American Revolution.

**Saint Elmo Brady for Outstanding Achievement in Science**

ThankGod Ugochukw

[![Image 13: Charles Watson and ThankGod Ugochukwu.](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/WatsonUgochukwu0010-1.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/WatsonUgochukwu0010-1.jpg)

Charles Watson, assistant director of diversity in the College of Engineering, and ThankGod Ugochukwu. Photo by Michael Salerno

ThankGod Ugochukw, of **Norwood, Mass**., is a biomedical engineering major. He’s been involved in the Louis Stokes Alliance for Minorities Participation Program, and that has afforded him various opportunities, including conducting research in the biomeasurement and biomedical instrumentation design labs. He interned with 21 st Century Fox, where he helped the engineering team repair damaged technology and worked on interactive programs. He’s been an integral part of the National Society of Black Engineers, serving as president this year.

**David Edmonds Award**

Sierra Jade Clayton, of **Providence**, is a writing and rhetoric major. She is an

[![Image 14: Bob Dilworth and Sierra Jade Clayton](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/DilworthClayton0009.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/DilworthClayton0009.jpg)

Bob Dilworth, art professor, and Sierra Jade Clayton. Photo by Michael Salerno

effective communicator who has demonstrated the ability to establish and maintain sensitive and equitable interpersonal relations, evidenced by her varied experiences working with culturally diverse groups. She is a member of the Rhode Island Chapter of the Lead Program and the National Coalition of 100 Black Women and New Urban Arts, and she is a volunteer for the Diversifying Individuals Via Education Conference. At New Urban Arts, she worked in the development of poetry, fashion, sketching, screen-printing and photography. She also has served as a senior consultant at the Writing and Rhetoric Lab at URI.

**Estes Benson Awards**

[![Image 15: Bryan Dewsbury and Florette Fils Aima, sister of Carine M. Saint Felix.](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/DewsburyFils-Aima0013.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/DewsburyFils-Aima0013.jpg)

Bryan Dewsbury, assistant professor biological sciences, and Florette Fils Aima, sister of Carine M. Saint Felix. Photo by Michael Salerno

Carine M. Saint Felix, a native of **Leogane, Haiti** who lives in **Woonsocket**, is a nursing major. She decided to become a nurse after losing her younger brother, who died suddenly after complaining of cold-like symptoms and was unable to get adequate health care in Haiti. Among her honors and involvement include the Sigma Theta Tau International Honor Society of Nursing; American Psychiatric Nurses Association; American Nurses Association; and Mentor/Educator-Women’s Refugee Center of Rhode Island. After completing her degree, she plans to pursue her master of science degree in nursing.

[![Image 16: Bryan Dewsbury and Pa Sosseh](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/DewsburySosseh0014.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news-draft/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/DewsburySosseh0014.jpg)

Bryan Dewsbury, assistant professor biological sciences, and Pa Sosseh. Photos by Michael Salerno

Pa Sosseh, a native of **Gambia**who lives in**Pawtucket**, came to the United States in 2010 and not long after that, enrolled at the Community College of Rhode Island. Seeking a way to pay tuition, Sosseh joined the Rhode Island National Guard. After completing his basic combat training, Sosseh transferred to URI, where he’s made the Dean’s List every semester. He initially majored in biochemistry, but after a research project through a science and engineering fellowship, he found his passion for molecular biology. He changed his major to medical laboratory science, with the goal of becoming a doctor.

Alycia Mosley Austin, assistant dean for recruitment and diversity initiatives at the Graduate School, and Danielle Perry. Photo by Michael Salerno

**Donald Cunnigen Award**

Danielle Perry, of **Hazlet, N.J**., is a third-year Ph.D. student in the biological and environmental sciences program. Her work focuses on the environmental stressors impacting coastal ecosystems. In addition to her research interests in marine conservation, Perry interns at the Save the Bay Center in Westerly. She mentors undergraduates through the RI-EPSCoR Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship program and as a teaching assistant in the College of the Environmental and Life Sciences. She strives to expose young people of color to opportunities in science, technology, engineering and math careers.

# Open Access Master's Theses

The University of Rhode Island archives and provides access to master's theses through DigitalCommons@URI. Theses prior to 2013 may or may not be available here. Please consult the [URI library catalog](https://web.uri.edu/library/) to see all titles. For those theses available only in print, the library can usually scan a copy upon request.

For scanning requests and all other questions about theses in DigitalCommons@URI, contact Julia Lovett, Digital Initiatives Librarian, at [jalovett@uri.edu](mailto:jalovett@uri.edu).

For questions about URI's thesis submission process in general, contact Al Gerheim at [gerheim@uri.edu](mailto:gerheim@uri.edu) or see [https://web.uri.edu/graduate-school/academics/thesis-dissertation/formatting/](https://web.uri.edu/graduate-school/academics/thesis-dissertation/formatting/).

# Open Access Master's Theses

The University of Rhode Island archives and provides access to master's theses through DigitalCommons@URI. Theses prior to 2013 may or may not be available here. Please consult the [URI library catalog](https://web.uri.edu/library/) to see all titles. For those theses available only in print, the library can usually scan a copy upon request.

For scanning requests and all other questions about theses in DigitalCommons@URI, contact Julia Lovett, Digital Initiatives Librarian, at [jalovett@uri.edu](mailto:jalovett@uri.edu).

# URI engineering professor named to PBN’s 40 Under Forty list

Gretchen Macht recognized for her work in systems engineering

[![Image 2: Gretchen Macht](https://www.uri.edu/news/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/Gretchen-Macht-in-lab.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/Gretchen-Macht-in-lab.jpg)

Assistant Professor Gretchen Macht in the Sustainable Innovation Solutions Lab. URI photo by Ayla Fox 

KINGSTON, R.I. – June 11, 2019 — The Providence Business News has named University of Rhode Island Assistant Professor Gretchen Macht to its[2019 40 Under Forty](https://pbn.com/event/2019-forty-under-40/) list.

The list recognizes individuals under the age of 40 who have excelled in their chosen profession and are involved in their communities.

“I am truly honored to receive this recognition,” said Macht, who has taught systems engineering at URI since 2015. “I attribute my success to the research I’ve conducted in the Sustainable Innovative Solutions (SIS) Laboratory and the support I’ve received from my family and the URI community.”

In the SIS Lab, Macht and her students use technology to research sustainable systems that are based on human factors, such as how people think and behave.

One project Macht worked on in the last year was RI VOTES (Voter OperaTions & Election Systems). With the goal of streamlining the voting process in Rhode Island, Macht and her team used technology to examine the source of delays at voting precincts.

“Gretchen is applying engineering to some of the greatest challenges to sustainability of our time,” said URI College of Engineering Dean Raymond Wright. “Her work is interdisciplinary and novel. It’s wonderful to see this recognition.”

Macht and the other 40 Under Forty honorees will be recognized at an event at Aldrich Mansion in Warwick on July 18.

Two years ago,Kunal Mankodiya, an assistant professor in URI’s Department of Electrical, Computer and Biomedical Engineering, received the PBN honor.

# URI engineering professor named to PBN’s 40 Under Forty list

Gretchen Macht recognized for her work in systems engineering

[![Image 2: Gretchen Macht](https://www.uri.edu/news/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/Gretchen-Macht-in-lab.jpg)](https://www.uri.edu/news/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2021/05/Gretchen-Macht-in-lab.jpg)

Assistant Professor Gretchen Macht in the Sustainable Innovation Solutions Lab. URI photo by Ayla Fox 

KINGSTON, R.I. – June 11, 2019 — The Providence Business News has named University of Rhode Island Assistant Professor Gretchen Macht to its[2019 40 Under Forty](https://pbn.com/event/2019-forty-under-40/) list.

The list recognizes individuals under the age of 40 who have excelled in their chosen profession and are involved in their communities.

“I am truly honored to receive this recognition,” said Macht, who has taught systems engineering at URI since 2015. “I attribute my success to the research I’ve conducted in the Sustainable Innovative Solutions (SIS) Laboratory and the support I’ve received from my family and the URI community.”

In the SIS Lab, Macht and her students use technology to research sustainable systems that are based on human factors, such as how people think and behave.

One project Macht worked on in the last year was RI VOTES (Voter OperaTions & Election Systems). With the goal of streamlining the voting process in Rhode Island, Macht and her team used technology to examine the source of delays at voting precincts.

“Gretchen is applying engineering to some of the greatest challenges to sustainability of our time,” said URI College of Engineering Dean Raymond Wright. “Her work is interdisciplinary and novel. It’s wonderful to see this recognition.”

Macht and the other 40 Under Forty honorees will be recognized at an event at Aldrich Mansion in Warwick on July 18.

Two years ago,Kunal Mankodiya, an assistant professor in URI’s Department of Electrical, Computer and Biomedical Engineering, received the PBN honor.

2026 ABSTRACT 

This study examines the ideological development and political significance of the Blueshirt movement in the Irish Free State, focusing mainly on how the transnational fascist thought developed amidst local conditions. It argues that although the Blueshirts, associated with organizations such as the Army Comrades Association (ACA) under the leadership of Eoin O'Duffy, incorporated aesthetic and ideological features of other interwar European fascisms into their program, including palingenetic ultranationalism, corporatism, and paramilitarism, these elements developed within the context of Ireland’s postcolonial political culture. These ideas were rooted in commonly held anti-British sentiment, which linked fascist politics of resentment and national regeneration to the legacy of colonial oppression, and the lingering tensions of the Irish Civil War. 

Through an analysis of their rhetoric, development, and transnational connections, this thesis demonstrates how the Blueshirts mobilized the legacies of oppression under British rule and the divisions of the Irish Civil War to legitimize their program. It then situates the movement within a broader network of European fascism, highlighting O’Duffy’s international ties and Irish participation in broader fascist discourses. Ultimately, this study will show how international fascist trends grew from local circumstances. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

INTRODUCTION 

On August 13, 1933, a grand parade was planned in Dublin. An estimated three-thousand members of General Eoin O’Duffy’s Army Comrades Association (ACA) would march on the city to honor “three great leaders”: Arthur Griffith, Michael Collins, and Kevin O’Higgins. 1 The three politicians had all advocated for the adoption of an Anglo-Irish treaty granting the new Irish Free State dominion status within the British Empire following the 1919-1920 War for Independence, a stance that ultimately led to the 1922-1923 Irish Civil War between pro- and anti-Treaty forces. It was during this Civil War that Griffith died of natural causes and Collins was assassinated; Higgins was later killed by anti-treaty forces in 1927. 2 The Blueshirts believed these men were heroes due to their service in the War for Independence and their pivotal roles in securing the treaty and independence for Ireland, but argued that “the State they died to succour” failed to properly honor them. 3

The ACA decided to take matters into their own hands. Their commemorative parade would stop in front of the Irish Parliament building to lay wreaths honoring Griffith, Collins, and O’Higgins before continuing on to the Glasnevin Cemetery, where O’Duffy would deliver a final address at Collins’s grave. 4 Participants were instructed to wear their uniforms of blue dress shirts, black ties, and berets and to carry walking sticks with them. 5 In an August 12 issue of The Blueshirt, the ACA’s newspaper, the parade’s

The contradiction between a planned commemorative parade framed as a patriotic act, a leader’s denial that his organization was fascist, and that same leader’s simultaneous engagement with continental fascist movements illustrates the central problem this thesis addresses. The ACA did imitate the aesthetic elements of other European fascisms, and, as this thesis will demonstrate, incorporate broader ideological trends common to interwar fascisms, like palingenetic ultranationalism, transcendent corporate-statism, and paramilitarism into its political program. 

The tension between these two elements — transnational influence and local politics and culture — was inherent to the Blueshirt movement. This thesis therefore argues that anti-British sentiment played a central role in shaping key elements of the movement’s ideology, rhetoric, and political agenda by connecting the fascist politics of resentment and revenge to the legacy of anti-imperialism and the Irish Civil War in the Irish Free State. Because the memories of British occupation and the fierce Civil War that erupted following Irish independence were fresh in the minds of Irishmen, the Blueshirts developed their fascist ideology within the context of these two events. By presenting the fascist principles or corporatism, anti-communism, paramilitarism, and regenerative ultranationalism within the pre-existing context of postcolonial Irish politics, specifically in publications meant for the Irish public like newspapers and pamphlets, the Blueshirts attempted to recruit Irish patriots to their cause. The following chapters will examine the construction and functions of Irish fascism. Following a review of the literature on both the Blueshirts as an organization and the larger field of fascist studies, the second chapter will examine the emergence of the Blueshirts within the political culture of the early Irish Free State, tracing how memories of British domination, the struggle for independence, and the legacy of the Irish Civil War shaped the movement’s rhetoric. Chapter III analyzes the ideology and agenda of the Blueshirts by focusing on how widely-held anti-British sentiment legitimized the promotion of a corporatist state, anti-communist policies, paramilitary violence, and regenerative ultranationalism. Finally, chapter IV will examine transnational connections of the Blueshirts, including O’Duffy’s relationships with European fascist leaders and the participation of Irish volunteers in conflicts such as the Spanish Civil War to demonstrate how the Blueshirts operated within a larger network of international fascisms. Together, these chapters will show that the Blueshirts represent a case in which fascist ideas were adapted to a post-colonial national context as well as the interactions between global and local politics during the interwar era. 

The majority of primary sources consulted for this thesis are publications meant for a general audience of both Blueshirt members and non-members. Newspapers, namely The Blueshirt and United Ireland, as well as speeches and pamphlets were forums through which Blueshirt leaders and thinkers could spread their rhetoric. As such, these sources were cloaked with anti-British sentiment. Situating their ideas within this sentiment, one that characterized Irish political discourses of the twentieth century, thus 

5allowed them to present fascist ideas not as fascist or imitations of the Italian or German cases, but as fundamentally Irish solutions to lingering British influence and the resurrection of Irish national identity. 14 Other primary sources include debates from the Dáil Eireann — the lower house of Ireland’s parliament — police reports, and the letters and personal writings of Blueshirt leadership. 

It is important to note that “the Blueshirts” was not an official name of any one organization. Rather, the term was used to describe the rank and file membership of multiple organizations led by O’Duffy, including the ACA (which was later refashioned as the National Guard), Fine Gael (a political party merging O’Duffy’s organizations with other conservatives), and the League of Youth (an alternate name for any one of these organizations meant to emphasize their dedication to creating a new Ireland), amongst others. Not all of these organizations were inherently fascist or even led solely by O’Duffy — Fine Gael, for example, ousted O’Duffy in 1934 due to his anti-democratic beliefs — but were vehicles through which the General spread fascist and corporatist ideas in the Irish Free State.

Early Emphasis on Fascism and Nazism 

The 1970s presented a shift in scholarly understandings of fascism, with historians Renzo De Felice and George Mosse attempting to develop new analytical frameworks that moved beyond earlier authoritarian and Marxist interpretations but still operating primarily through the lens of Italian Fascism and Nazism. De Felice was amongst the first to suggest that a new interpretive model was necessary in his 1977 

Interpretations of Fascism, acknowledging that fascism spread across the European continent during the interwar era, and was not necessarily confined to Germany or Italy. He warned, however, that leaning too much into the interpretation of fascism as a “phenomenon of supranational dimensions” would “underestimate the significance of specific historical circumstances in the various countries where Fascism emerged.” 17 

Creating too narrow a definition of fascism, he argued, would make it difficult to understand why fascism was so popular amongst the European masses. 18 De Felice believed that a happy medium between the rigidity of previous interpretations and more general typologies would position fascism as a European phenomenon “brought about by World War I and [in response] to the moral and material crisis occasioned by conversion to a mass society with new political and social institutions.” 19 De Felice’s fascism was

A more global, or transnational, approach to fascist studies has emerged, moving away from centering the continental European manifestations of the phenomenon. Only Germany was seen as the successor to the Holy Roman Empire, just like Italy was seen as the progeny of the original western Roman Empire. Julia Adeney Thomas also argued for a transnational understanding of fascism, stating that “fascism is not best understood by creating particularistic models that focus on single nations or by abstracting a Eurocentric version of the populist Right and applying it elsewhere.” 49 Rather, she argued, fascism’s “protean qualities made opposition all the more difficult, and it could travel the world more freely.” 50 The malleability of fascism as a broad, general set of ideas and attitudes, then, is what made its spread so easy. Any country facing any sort of internal instability could galvanize local resentments to fit in with a more flexible set of fascist ideals.

“HATREDS, BETRAYALS, AND DISILLUSIONMENT”: THE BLUESHIRTS IN IRISH HISTORICAL CONTEXT 

The Blueshirts did not emerge in a vacuum of solely Irish circumstances, nor were they solely an imitation of continental fascism. Rather, the movement developed within the political culture of the Irish Free State, shaped by centuries of oppression under British rule, the fight for independence, and a Civil War that divided revolutionary politics. This chapter argues that the Blueshirts must be understood as a product of these legacies. While the ideology and rhetoric of the movement echoed those of continental movements, the Blueshirt program was shaped not by foreign tensions but internal ones. By examining the politics of the early Irish Free State, we can see how anti-British sentiment and resentment and continued tensions between the two opposing factions of the Civil War shaped Blueshirt thought. 

Ireland’s Colonial Past 

The British presence in Ireland began in the eleventh century following Anglo-Norman interference in an Irish conflict. 65 English authority was asserted in 1171 when Henry II of England arrived and claimed lordship over the island. English control and settlement was initially limited to an area surrounding Dublin called the Pale, and by

The sixteenth century, however, marked the beginning of harsher enforcement of English authority. In the 1530s, King Henry VIII began a series of conquests beyond Dublin, and was met with significant resistance by the native Irish population. In 1534, Thomas FitzGerald, also known as “Silken Thomas,” led a rebellion against the English by declaring loyalty to the Pope and the Catholic Church and calling for English expulsion from Ireland. Thomas’s revolt was defeated in 1537, and in 1541, Henry III formally declared himself King of Ireland and began implementing English law and political administration on the island. 

Subsequent monarchs established a plantation system in the northern province of Ulster, meant to settle British and Scottish elites to secure English political hegemony and spread Protestantism. Land was confiscated from Catholics and reissued to settlers, creating a colonial system which saw Irish Catholics severely disenfranchised. Later legislation banned Catholics from owning land altogether, holding public office, owning guns, or practicing law. 67 These Penal Laws even attempted to limit the practice of Catholicism, though such rules were rarely enforced. 68 The Acts of Union, passed in 1801, fully subordinated the Irish population through the abolishment of an extremely weak Irish Parliament, ensuring that the Irish had no representation within the British Empire. 69

23 Resistance and Nationalism 

The loss of political autonomy, the “ascendancy” of the Protestant elite, and the restriction of Catholic civil rights following the adoption of the Acts of Union all worked together to create a clearer sense of Irish nationalism in the nineteenth century, as independence from British domination was increasingly viewed as the only way to protect Irish land, rights, and religious identity. Several political parties and lobbies developed in the late nineteenth century, seeking to secure Irish autonomy through different avenues. The Home Government Association, later known as the Irish Parliamentary Party (IPP) was established by Isaac Butt in 1870 and sought to secure autonomy for Ireland. 70 Through a system of “home rule,” as the IPP termed it, Ireland would remain a part of the United Kingdom but would have control of its own domestic affairs. 71 Several bills were introduced in the British Parliament to grant Ireland home rule. The first two, introduced in 1886 and 1893, were vetoed, while a third bill was passed in 1914 but ultimately halted due to Britain’s entry into the First World War. 

By the turn of the century, some Irish nationalists saw the IPP’s emphasis on negotiation and cooperation with the British government as being not only ineffective but highly hypocritical. Another organization known as the Fenians, or Irish Republican Brotherhood (IRB), grew in popularity as a result. Although the IRB had been active since the 1850s, the IPP’s failure to secure home rule turned more and more nationalists towards the IRB’s more radical policies. 72 The IRB was far more militant in its approach than the IPP and did not believe in the power of political maneuvering. 36 CHAPTER III 

“IRISH NEEDS AND CULTURE”: CHARACTERISTICS OF FASCISM IN THE IRISH FREE STATE 

As the last chapter showed, the Blueshirts were not an imported fascist movement based upon continental models. They emerged in a post-independence, post-Civil War Irish Free State and were therefore shaped by the anti-British sentiment and lingering tensions between pro- and anti-treaty forces. 

This does not mean, however, that a fascist identification does not fit the Blueshirts. On the contrary — several core elements of their rhetoric and ideology were aligned with those of other fascisms. These elements were not copied from other fascisms, but were rather natural progressions of the anti-British politics of the Irish Free State. The Blueshirt emphasis on corporate statism, anti-communism, paramilitary violence, and regenerative ultranationalism, particularly in their publications, was not born from their desire to mimic continental movements. Rather, these fascist principles were emphasized as tools in the continuing popular struggle against British influence. 

In European Fascist Movements: A Sourcebook, Roland Clark and Tim Grady described fascism as being an “empty signifier.” Although the fascist label functions as a categorization tool, connecting different fascisms to one another, “contemporaries did not experience fascism as a series of connected movements nor as a transnational movement with local branches. Instead, they saw fascism as a ‘wave’ sweeping Europe.” 122

62 The ideological program of the Blueshirts demonstrates how fascist principles were legitimized within local contexts. Corporatism, anti-communism, and regenerative ultranationalism were not embraced by the Blueshirts because they were elements of foreign fascisms and therefore needed to emulate successful regimes, but because they were seen as effective tools for resisting British influence. By positioning these ideas within the tradition of revolutionary nationalism, the Blueshirts presented fascist solutions as being inherently Irish in character. Analyzing the Blueshirts as a derivative movement of continental fascisms therefore obscures the role Irish history and traditions played in shaping their program. Fascist principles were seen as a legitimately Irish way to solve the problems that had found their origin either in British presence or anti-treaty efforts to destroy Ireland. Resentment of British politics led Irish fascists to adopt corporatist policies. Additionally, Irish Catholicism — a cornerstone of the Irish national identity that developed in the nineteenth century — pushed them towards the corporatist system, and, equally as important, away from communism. Their framing of Fianna Fáil as communists was a manifestation of global fascisms’ fear of the ideology, but also acted as an extension of Civil War tensions. Similarly, paramilitary violence enacted both by and against the Blueshirts was merely a continuation of anti- and pro-treaty clashes. Finally, regenerative ultranationalism was a way to fight back against the legacies of British imperialism by reintroducing what the Blueshirts claimed to be traditional Irish values that had been crushed by centuries of colonial rule. Although the defining characteristics of the Blueshirts aligned them with continental movements, we cannot understand them as being simply an imitation. Their values and program were rooted in both anti-British sentiment and continued resentment towards their Civil War foes. 

63 CHAPTER IV 

SUBSTANCE, STYLE, AND THE SYMBOLIC: TRANSNATIONAL BLUESHIRT CONNECTIONS 

When considering whether or not the Blueshirts were truly a fascist organization, Manning argued that, despite their stylistic similarities to fascist movements, they possessed “little enough of the substance” of actual fascisms to warrant such a classification. 236 Manning contended that although the Blueshirts had adopted the shirted uniforms and Roman salute of continental fascisms, their program did not align with those of, say, the Italian Fascists or the Nazis and was instead the product of Ireland’s political landscape. 

Manning’s argument, however, did not fully address the nuances of Blueshirt ideology. The movement was not just fascist or just Irish, but an Irish strain of fascism shaped by anti-British sentiment and consequently Civil War tensions. While the visual aesthetic of the Blueshirts was their most obvious similarity to other fascisms, their core ideology of corporatism, anti-communism, and regenerative ultranationalism aligned them with the larger trends of interwar fascism. Still, their connections to and engagements with other fascist movements should not be ignored. The adoption of raised-arm salutes and colored uniforms was obviously the most visible, but O’Duffy’s connections to international fascist leaders also provided the Blueshirts with a sense of international validation and belonging within a larger ideological movement that increasingly influenced the geopolitical environment of continental Europe and the entire world, for that matter.

64 It was not only shared ideology that connected the Blueshirts to international allies. The resentment the Blueshirts held towards the British was echoed around the world, with countless fascisms seeing their system as a way to exact revenge on an order that had deprived them of prosperity. Thus, the Blueshirts’ international connections legitimized not only their policies, but also their emotional stake in the implementation of fascism. 

Fascist Aesthetics 

While broad ideological trends connected fascist movements regardless of how they were situated within local conditions, many interwar organizations shared a common visual and symbolic language. If any aspect of Italian Fascism or Nazism could be considered to have been “imitated” by other fascisms, it was their aesthetics. Uniforms, salutes, insignia, and mass demonstrations created a recognizable political style that could be transported anywhere in the world regardless of diverse local cultures and concerns. Rather than shaping the social or economic character of individual movements — traits that were heavily dependent upon the unique problems each hoped to solve within their own countries — fascist aesthetics served to create a unified “civic religion” for members. 237 According to George Mosse, Europe had entered a “visual age” at the end of the long nineteenth century, when symbols such as flags or anthems became associated with politics (in this case, nationalist politics). 238 Symbols could act as a unifier, then, and fascist movements utilized them in constructing their civic religions in ways that other political movements did not. 2026 ABSTRACT 

This study examines the ideological development and political significance of the Blueshirt movement in the Irish Free State, focusing mainly on how the transnational fascist thought developed amidst local conditions. It argues that although the Blueshirts, associated with organizations such as the Army Comrades Association (ACA) under the leadership of Eoin O'Duffy, incorporated aesthetic and ideological features of other interwar European fascisms into their program, including palingenetic ultranationalism, corporatism, and paramilitarism, these elements developed within the context of Ireland’s postcolonial political culture. These ideas were rooted in commonly held anti-British sentiment, which linked fascist politics of resentment and national regeneration to the legacy of colonial oppression, and the lingering tensions of the Irish Civil War. 

Through an analysis of their rhetoric, development, and transnational connections, this thesis demonstrates how the Blueshirts mobilized the legacies of oppression under British rule and the divisions of the Irish Civil War to legitimize their program. It then situates the movement within a broader network of European fascism, highlighting O’Duffy’s international ties and Irish participation in broader fascist discourses. Ultimately, this study will show how international fascist trends grew from local circumstances. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

INTRODUCTION 

On August 13, 1933, a grand parade was planned in Dublin. An estimated three-thousand members of General Eoin O’Duffy’s Army Comrades Association (ACA) would march on the city to honor “three great leaders”: Arthur Griffith, Michael Collins, and Kevin O’Higgins. 1 The three politicians had all advocated for the adoption of an Anglo-Irish treaty granting the new Irish Free State dominion status within the British Empire following the 1919-1920 War for Independence, a stance that ultimately led to the 1922-1923 Irish Civil War between pro- and anti-Treaty forces. It was during this Civil War that Griffith died of natural causes and Collins was assassinated; Higgins was later killed by anti-treaty forces in 1927. 2 The Blueshirts believed these men were heroes due to their service in the War for Independence and their pivotal roles in securing the treaty and independence for Ireland, but argued that “the State they died to succour” failed to properly honor them. 3

The ACA decided to take matters into their own hands. Their commemorative parade would stop in front of the Irish Parliament building to lay wreaths honoring Griffith, Collins, and O’Higgins before continuing on to the Glasnevin Cemetery, where O’Duffy would deliver a final address at Collins’s grave. 4 Participants were instructed to wear their uniforms of blue dress shirts, black ties, and berets and to carry walking sticks with them. 5 In an August 12 issue of The Blueshirt, the ACA’s newspaper, the parade’s

The following chapters will examine the construction and functions of Irish fascism. Following a review of the literature on both the Blueshirts as an organization and the larger field of fascist studies, the second chapter will examine the emergence of the Blueshirts within the political culture of the early Irish Free State, tracing how memories of British domination, the struggle for independence, and the legacy of the Irish Civil War shaped the movement’s rhetoric. Chapter III analyzes the ideology and agenda of the Blueshirts by focusing on how widely-held anti-British sentiment legitimized the promotion of a corporatist state, anti-communist policies, paramilitary violence, and regenerative ultranationalism. Finally, chapter IV will examine transnational connections of the Blueshirts, including O’Duffy’s relationships with European fascist leaders and the participation of Irish volunteers in conflicts such as the Spanish Civil War to demonstrate how the Blueshirts operated within a larger network of international fascisms. Together, these chapters will show that the Blueshirts represent a case in which fascist ideas were adapted to a post-colonial national context as well as the interactions between global and local politics during the interwar era. 

The majority of primary sources consulted for this thesis are publications meant for a general audience of both Blueshirt members and non-members. Newspapers, namely The Blueshirt and United Ireland, as well as speeches and pamphlets were forums through which Blueshirt leaders and thinkers could spread their rhetoric. As such, these sources were cloaked with anti-British sentiment. Situating their ideas within this sentiment, one that characterized Irish political discourses of the twentieth century, thus 

5allowed them to present fascist ideas not as fascist or imitations of the Italian or German cases, but as fundamentally Irish solutions to lingering British influence and the resurrection of Irish national identity. 14 Other primary sources include debates from the Dáil Eireann — the lower house of Ireland’s parliament — police reports, and the letters and personal writings of Blueshirt leadership. 

It is important to note that “the Blueshirts” was not an official name of any one organization. Rather, the term was used to describe the rank and file membership of multiple organizations led by O’Duffy, including the ACA (which was later refashioned as the National Guard), Fine Gael (a political party merging O’Duffy’s organizations with other conservatives), and the League of Youth (an alternate name for any one of these organizations meant to emphasize their dedication to creating a new Ireland), amongst others. Not all of these organizations were inherently fascist or even led solely by O’Duffy — Fine Gael, for example, ousted O’Duffy in 1934 due to his anti-democratic beliefs — but were vehicles through which the General spread fascist and corporatist ideas in the Irish Free State.

Payne’s typology, then, expanded the definition of fascism to include other movements and regimes. “HATREDS, BETRAYALS, AND DISILLUSIONMENT”: THE BLUESHIRTS IN IRISH HISTORICAL CONTEXT 

The Blueshirts did not emerge in a vacuum of solely Irish circumstances, nor were they solely an imitation of continental fascism. Rather, the movement developed within the political culture of the Irish Free State, shaped by centuries of oppression under British rule, the fight for independence, and a Civil War that divided revolutionary politics. This chapter argues that the Blueshirts must be understood as a product of these legacies. While the ideology and rhetoric of the movement echoed those of continental movements, the Blueshirt program was shaped not by foreign tensions but internal ones. By examining the politics of the early Irish Free State, we can see how anti-British sentiment and resentment and continued tensions between the two opposing factions of the Civil War shaped Blueshirt thought. 

Ireland’s Colonial Past 

The British presence in Ireland began in the eleventh century following Anglo-Norman interference in an Irish conflict. 65 English authority was asserted in 1171 when Henry II of England arrived and claimed lordship over the island. English control and settlement was initially limited to an area surrounding Dublin called the Pale, and by    

> 65 Richard Killeen, A Brief History of Ireland: Land, People, History (Running Press, 2012), 43-45.

22 the fifteenth century, many of those early settlers had adopted the Irish language and customs. 66 

The sixteenth century, however, marked the beginning of harsher enforcement of English authority. In the 1530s, King Henry VIII began a series of conquests beyond Dublin, and was met with significant resistance by the native Irish population. In 1534, Thomas FitzGerald, also known as “Silken Thomas,” led a rebellion against the English by declaring loyalty to the Pope and the Catholic Church and calling for English expulsion from Ireland. Thomas’s revolt was defeated in 1537, and in 1541, Henry III formally declared himself King of Ireland and began implementing English law and political administration on the island. 

Subsequent monarchs established a plantation system in the northern province of Ulster, meant to settle British and Scottish elites to secure English political hegemony and spread Protestantism. Land was confiscated from Catholics and reissued to settlers, creating a colonial system which saw Irish Catholics severely disenfranchised. Later legislation banned Catholics from owning land altogether, holding public office, owning guns, or practicing law. 67 These Penal Laws even attempted to limit the practice of Catholicism, though such rules were rarely enforced. 68 The Acts of Union, passed in 1801, fully subordinated the Irish population through the abolishment of an extremely weak Irish Parliament, ensuring that the Irish had no representation within the British Empire. 69

The loss of political autonomy, the “ascendancy” of the Protestant elite, and the restriction of Catholic civil rights following the adoption of the Acts of Union all worked together to create a clearer sense of Irish nationalism in the nineteenth century, as independence from British domination was increasingly viewed as the only way to protect Irish land, rights, and religious identity. Several political parties and lobbies developed in the late nineteenth century, seeking to secure Irish autonomy through different avenues. The Home Government Association, later known as the Irish Parliamentary Party (IPP) was established by Isaac Butt in 1870 and sought to secure autonomy for Ireland. 70 Through a system of “home rule,” as the IPP termed it, Ireland would remain a part of the United Kingdom but would have control of its own domestic affairs. 71 Several bills were introduced in the British Parliament to grant Ireland home rule. The first two, introduced in 1886 and 1893, were vetoed, while a third bill was passed in 1914 but ultimately halted due to Britain’s entry into the First World War. 

By the turn of the century, some Irish nationalists saw the IPP’s emphasis on negotiation and cooperation with the British government as being not only ineffective but highly hypocritical. Another organization known as the Fenians, or Irish Republican Brotherhood (IRB), grew in popularity as a result. Although the IRB had been active since the 1850s, the IPP’s failure to secure home rule turned more and more nationalists towards the IRB’s more radical policies. 72 The IRB was far more militant in its approach than the IPP and did not believe in the power of political maneuvering. Both versions of the Blueshirt constitution show that the movement’s ideology was a continuation of Irish politics rather than a completely foreign import. The Blueshirts emerged in a political arena shaped by centuries of oppression under British rule. The revolutionary politics of the late-nineteenth and early-twentieth centuries were centered upon the procurement of liberation from British domination, making the construction and embrace of a cohesive national identity a key element of their programs. The Blueshirts were no different than the political parties that came before them and existed at the same time as them. Even the promotion of corporatism, a cornerstone of Italian Fascism, was reframed by O’Duffy as being uniquely suited to Irish culture rather than a carbon copy of Mussolini’s program. 

Analyzing the Blueshirts solely through a transnational fascist framework therefore ignores the domestic conditions that necessitated the creation of the organization and shaped its character. Rather than a copy-and-pasted version of continental movements, the Blueshirts were a product of the political and historical conditions of the Irish Free State. Resentment towards the British had been characteristic of Irish revolutionary politics since their development in the nineteenth century, and the desire to break from British influence characterized both the Blueshirts and their rivals. Perhaps more useful in understanding the development of the Blueshirts, however, is the context of intense distrust and hatred between the pro- and anti-treaty Civil War factions. 36 CHAPTER III 

“IRISH NEEDS AND CULTURE”: CHARACTERISTICS OF FASCISM IN THE IRISH FREE STATE 

As the last chapter showed, the Blueshirts were not an imported fascist movement based upon continental models. They emerged in a post-independence, post-Civil War Irish Free State and were therefore shaped by the anti-British sentiment and lingering tensions between pro- and anti-treaty forces. 

This does not mean, however, that a fascist identification does not fit the Blueshirts. On the contrary — several core elements of their rhetoric and ideology were aligned with those of other fascisms. These elements were not copied from other fascisms, but were rather natural progressions of the anti-British politics of the Irish Free State. The Blueshirt emphasis on corporate statism, anti-communism, paramilitary violence, and regenerative ultranationalism, particularly in their publications, was not born from their desire to mimic continental movements. Rather, these fascist principles were emphasized as tools in the continuing popular struggle against British influence. 

In European Fascist Movements: A Sourcebook, Roland Clark and Tim Grady described fascism as being an “empty signifier.” Although the fascist label functions as a categorization tool, connecting different fascisms to one another, “contemporaries did not experience fascism as a series of connected movements nor as a transnational movement with local branches. Instead, they saw fascism as a ‘wave’ sweeping Europe.” 122 

According to Clark and Grady, movements could have viewed fascist principles as being

Corporatism 

Two of the characteristics of fascism identified by Michael Mann were transcendence and statism. According to Mann, “fascists worshipped state power” and believed that only through a corporate system of state government could the social, economic, and moral crises of the twentieth century be solved. 124

Paramilitary Violence 

Paramilitarism was identified as a key component of fascism by Michael Mann. A violent “bottom-up” approach characterized most organizations’ approaches to law enforcement and cleansing, especially when they were not in power. 169 O’Duffy did not have control of the Garda Síochána or the military, so any force he raised to combat communist activities would operate outside of the state apparatus. Maurice Manning argued that, despite Blueshirt leadership “exhorting members to be prepared for combat,” they “never sought or hoped to gain their objectives through the use of force.” 170 

According to Manning, any violence that the Blueshirts did engage in was because Republican and Fianna Fáil had provoked them; Blueshirt fighting was a matter of self-defense, not a systematic method of asserting power. 171

Established originally to protect the meetings of Cumann na nGeadheal politicians from IRA members, the Blueshirts often defended the upper leadership of the organization from violence.
