62 The ideological program of the Blueshirts demonstrates how fascist principles were legitimized within local contexts. Corporatism, anti-communism, and regenerative ultranationalism were not embraced by the Blueshirts because they were elements of foreign fascisms and therefore needed to emulate successful regimes, but because they were seen as effective tools for resisting British influence. By positioning these ideas within the tradition of revolutionary nationalism, the Blueshirts presented fascist solutions as being inherently Irish in character. Analyzing the Blueshirts as a derivative movement of continental fascisms therefore obscures the role Irish history and traditions played in shaping their program. Fascist principles were seen as a legitimately Irish way to solve the problems that had found their origin either in British presence or anti-treaty efforts to destroy Ireland. Resentment of British politics led Irish fascists to adopt corporatist policies. Additionally, Irish Catholicism — a cornerstone of the Irish national identity that developed in the nineteenth century — pushed them towards the corporatist system, and, equally as important, away from communism. Their framing of Fianna Fáil as communists was a manifestation of global fascisms’ fear of the ideology, but also acted as an extension of Civil War tensions. Similarly, paramilitary violence enacted both by and against the Blueshirts was merely a continuation of anti- and pro-treaty clashes. Finally, regenerative ultranationalism was a way to fight back against the legacies of British imperialism by reintroducing what the Blueshirts claimed to be traditional Irish values that had been crushed by centuries of colonial rule. Although the defining characteristics of the Blueshirts aligned them with continental movements, we cannot understand them as being simply an imitation. Their values and program were rooted in both anti-British sentiment and continued resentment towards their Civil War foes. 

63 CHAPTER IV 

SUBSTANCE, STYLE, AND THE SYMBOLIC: TRANSNATIONAL BLUESHIRT CONNECTIONS 

When considering whether or not the Blueshirts were truly a fascist organization, Manning argued that, despite their stylistic similarities to fascist movements, they possessed “little enough of the substance” of actual fascisms to warrant such a classification. 236 Manning contended that although the Blueshirts had adopted the shirted uniforms and Roman salute of continental fascisms, their program did not align with those of, say, the Italian Fascists or the Nazis and was instead the product of Ireland’s political landscape. 

Manning’s argument, however, did not fully address the nuances of Blueshirt ideology. The movement was not just fascist or just Irish, but an Irish strain of fascism shaped by anti-British sentiment and consequently Civil War tensions. While the visual aesthetic of the Blueshirts was their most obvious similarity to other fascisms, their core ideology of corporatism, anti-communism, and regenerative ultranationalism aligned them with the larger trends of interwar fascism. Still, their connections to and engagements with other fascist movements should not be ignored. The adoption of raised-arm salutes and colored uniforms was obviously the most visible, but O’Duffy’s connections to international fascist leaders also provided the Blueshirts with a sense of international validation and belonging within a larger ideological movement that increasingly influenced the geopolitical environment of continental Europe and the entire world, for that matter.    

> 236 Manning, The Blueshirts ,244.

64 It was not only shared ideology that connected the Blueshirts to international allies. The resentment the Blueshirts held towards the British was echoed around the world, with countless fascisms seeing their system as a way to exact revenge on an order that had deprived them of prosperity. Thus, the Blueshirts’ international connections legitimized not only their policies, but also their emotional stake in the implementation of fascism. 

Fascist Aesthetics 

While broad ideological trends connected fascist movements regardless of how they were situated within local conditions, many interwar organizations shared a common visual and symbolic language. If any aspect of Italian Fascism or Nazism could be considered to have been “imitated” by other fascisms, it was their aesthetics. Uniforms, salutes, insignia, and mass demonstrations created a recognizable political style that could be transported anywhere in the world regardless of diverse local cultures and concerns. Rather than shaping the social or economic character of individual movements — traits that were heavily dependent upon the unique problems each hoped to solve within their own countries — fascist aesthetics served to create a unified “civic religion” for members. 237 According to George Mosse, Europe had entered a “visual age” at the end of the long nineteenth century, when symbols such as flags or anthems became associated with politics (in this case, nationalist politics). 238 Symbols could act as a unifier, then, and fascist movements utilized them in constructing their civic religions in ways that other political movements did not. Stanley Payne argued that “the great       

> 238 Mosse, The Fascist Revolution, 41.
> 237 Mosse, The Fascist Revolution, 39.

The Blueshirts certainly incorporated such liturgical elements into their organization. The most obvious of these was their adoption of, well, the light-blue button-up shirts as a uniform. Fascists in other countries had embraced this costuming — the Nazis had the Brownshirts, while Mussolini’s militia dressed in black shirts. “The blue shirt,” O’Duffy said, “like a flag, is not a mere piece of cloth. It is our emblem, our symbol, our ideal.” 240 

Even these uniforms, however, were chosen with Irish history and national culture in mind. When questioned by the New York Times about his selection of the color blue for his Guard’s uniforms rather than the green and orange typically associated with Ireland, O’Duffy said that Ireland’s “national color is blue, St. Patrick blue.” 241 The New York Times noted that while historical records supported O’Duffy’s claim, it was “not clear that there was any one national, military or governmental color in ancient Ireland.” 242 St. Patrick did represent Ireland’s ancient, Catholic past — a lost golden age that had existed prior to British influence. By dressing his National Guard in St. Patrick’s color, O’Duffy equated the movement with a return to the values of an Ireland that had been repressed.

Thousands of men marching on Dublin in matching uniforms certainly echoed the mass spectacle of fascist parades elsewhere in Europe. Blueshirts were also encouraged to wear their uniforms to meetings, making them easily identifiable to other Blueshirts and to the broader public. 244

…the wearing of uniforms in this country, as in other European countries, has resulted in the creation of disorders, and the creation of those disorders has imposed on the authorities a strain that the authorities cannot adequately deal with…. Those ideas about uniforms and blueshirts are not original in this country. The uniform, and indeed the objects of the organisation which dons the uniform, seem to have been copied, without practically a comma being changed, from similar organisations in Continental countries. Those Continental countries have had to deal with that situation. They have had to deal with what has been described as militarisation in politics. 246             

> 246 Dáil Éireann debate, 28 Feb 1934, Houses of the Oireachtas, https://www.oireachtas.ie/en/debates/debate/dail/1934-02-28/18/.
> 245 The Blueshirt, 5 Aug 1933.

Citing similar bills banning the wearing of shirted uniforms in Belgium, the Netherlands, Scandinavia, and the Baltic States, Ruttledge asserted that prohibiting the wearing of uniforms could successfully curb Blueshirt political ambitions and further violence. 247
